pronunciation.t: Urdu is written from right to left.
pronunciation.tip: Begin at the right edge; connected letters change shape by position.
Use romanisation and context while your sight vocabulary grows.

pronunciation.t: خ and غ are throat sounds.
pronunciation.tip: Let air rub gently in the throat; never strain.

pronunciation.t: ٹ ڈ ڑ use a curled tongue.
pronunciation.tip: Curl the tongue tip back briefly for these retroflex sounds.
Compare میں (main, I); let resonance pass through the nose.

alphabet.title: Urdu Nastaliq Script
alphabet.explain: Urdu is written right to left in the beautiful Nastaliq style — start at the RIGHT end of the line! Letters change shape (start/middle/end) and join up, there are no capital letters, and short vowels (a/i/u) are usually left unwritten: you read مل as 'mil' (meet) or 'mal' by context. Dots do heavy lifting: ب ت ث ن ی are the same stroke with different dots. Persian gave Urdu پ چ ژ گ, India gave it ٹ ڈ ڑ, and nasalization comes from ں (nūn-ghunna): میں (main, I) vs مین — count the dots, then read.

counting.title: Urdu Numbers 1–100
counting.explain: Urdu has no classifiers — put the number straight before the noun. But the noun itself goes plural: ایک کتاب (one book), دو کتابیں (two books), تین روپے (three rupees). Exactly like Hindi.
rules: Put the number before the noun: ایک کتاب (ek kitāb), one book.
Many counted nouns take a plural form: دو کتابیں (do kitāben), two books.

level.title: A1 Beginner Urdu
goals: Read and recognise the core Nastaliq letters from right to left.
Exchange greetings and handle essential daily interactions politely.
Build short present-tense sentences with clear romanisation support.

lessons.title: Greetings and Courtesy
lessons.learn: Begin with respectful Urdu greetings and survival courtesy. Read from right to left, use the romanisation as a bridge, and listen before repeating. آپ (āp) is the safe respectful form for a new person or an elder.

vocab.t: آپ سے مل کر خوشی ہوئی
vocab.r: Āp se mil kar khushī huī

grammar.title: Respectful introductions
grammar.explain: Use آپ (āp) for respectful “you.” A name is linked with ہے (hai), while a self-description with میں (main) commonly ends in ہوں (hūn).
mistakes: Do not use informal تم (tum) for an elder or a stranger.

dialogue.t: السلام علیکم! میرا نام احمد ہے۔
dialogue.r: Assalām Alaikum! Merā nām Ahmed hai.
dialogue.en: Peace be upon you! My name is Ahmed.

dialogue.t: وعلیکم السلام! میں فاطمہ۔ آپ کیسی ہیں؟
dialogue.r: Va Alaikum Assalām! Main Fātimā. Āp kaisī hain?
dialogue.en: And upon you peace! I'm Fatima. How are you?

dialogue.t: میں ٹھیک ہوں، شکریہ۔ آپ کہاں سے ہیں؟
dialogue.r: Main ṭhīk hūn, shukriyā. Āp kahān se hain?
dialogue.en: I'm fine, thanks. Where are you from?

dialogue.t: میں لکھنؤ سے ہوں۔ آپ کا شہر کون سا ہے؟
dialogue.r: Main Lakhnaū se hūn. Āp kā shahar kaun sā hai?
dialogue.en: I'm from Lucknow. Which city is yours?

quiz.why: آپ کا نام کیا ہے؟ (Āp kā nām kyā hai?) means “What is your name?.”

lessons.title: People, Names, and Pronouns
lessons.learn: Identify speakers and talk about names with basic pronouns. Urdu does not mark he and she with different pronouns: وہ (vo) can mean either, so context supplies gender.

grammar.title: Pronouns and politeness
grammar.explain: Urdu's آپ mirrors Hindi's aap; use it for respect.

lessons.title: Things, Places, and ہے
lessons.learn: Name familiar objects and places and build identification sentences with یہ (ye), وہ (vo), ہے (hai), and ہیں (hain). Urdu normally places the verb at the end.

grammar.title: Urdu word order
grammar.explain: Urdu is nearly identical to Hindi in structure: 'I water drink'.

dialogue.t: دادی، کھانا مہک رہا ہے!

lessons.title: Food and Simple Requests
lessons.learn: Name common foods and make child-safe, polite requests. Notice noun gender, but first learn useful complete expressions rather than guessing every ending.

grammar.title: Gender agreement
grammar.explain: Many adjectives ending in ا change to ی with a feminine noun. Memorise each noun with a model phrase, because noun gender is grammatical.
mistakes: Do not assume an object’s natural properties determine its grammatical gender.

dialogue.t: السلام علیکم! کیا لیں گے؟
dialogue.r: Assalām Alaikum! Kyā lenge?
dialogue.en: Greetings! What will you have?

dialogue.t: ہمیں دو پلیٹیں بریانی دیں۔ نہاری ہے؟
dialogue.r: Hamen do pleṭen biryānī den. Nahārī hai?
dialogue.en: Give us two plates of biryani. Do you have nihari?

dialogue.t: جی ہاں! نان کے ساتھ بہت مزہ آئے گا۔
dialogue.r: Jī hān! Nān ke sāth bahut mazā āegā.
dialogue.en: Yes indeed! It'll be delicious with naan.

dialogue.t: اچھا — ساتھ میں دو میٹھی لسیاں بھی۔
dialogue.r: Achchhā — sāth men do mīṭhī lassiyān bhī.
dialogue.en: Good — two sweet lassis with that too.

practice.q: Complete this model: This is good food.
practice.answer: یہ اچھا کھانا ہے۔ (ye achchhā khānā hai.)

lessons.title: Travel and Essential Questions
lessons.learn: Ask where something is, name transport, and request help politely. Question words remain near the information being requested, while the verb generally closes the sentence.

grammar.title: Questions with کہاں and کتنا
grammar.explain: Place کہاں (kahān, where) or کتنا (kitnā, how much) where the missing information belongs. Keep ہے (hai) at the end in a basic present question.
mistakes: Do not copy English do/does into Urdu questions; intonation and the question word do the work.

dialogue.t: السلام علیکم! یہ کرتا کتنے کا ہے؟
dialogue.r: Assalām Alaikum! Ye kurtā kitne kā hai?
dialogue.en: Greetings! How much is this kurta?

dialogue.t: پندرہ سو روپے کا ہے جی۔ بہت عمدہ چیز ہے۔
dialogue.r: Pandrah sau rupay kā hai jī. Bahut umdā chīz hai.
dialogue.en: Fifteen hundred rupees, sir. Very fine stuff.

dialogue.t: بہت مہنگا ہے! ہزار میں دیں۔
dialogue.r: Bahut mehangā hai! Hazār men den.
dialogue.en: Too expensive! Give it for a thousand.

dialogue.t: نہیں جی، بارہ سو سے کم نہیں ہوگا۔
dialogue.r: Nahīn jī, bārah sau se kam nahīn hogā.
dialogue.en: No sir, it won't go below twelve hundred.

lessons.title: Daily Actions and Present Tense
lessons.learn: Describe simple habits with present-tense verbs. The habitual ending agrees with gender and number, while ہوں, ہو, ہے, or ہیں agrees with the subject.
